claim: PTPRK is a transmembrane receptor that links extracellular homophilic interactions to intracellular catalytic activity.
source: Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor-type kappa (PTPRK) is a transmembrane receptor that links extracellular homophilic interactions to intracellular catalytic activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of PTPRK.

claim: PTPRK promotes cell–cell adhesion by selectively dephosphorylating several cell junction regulators including the protein Afadin.
source: Previously we showed that PTPRK promotes cell–cell adhesion by selectively dephosphorylating several cell junction regulators including the protein Afadin (Fearnley et al, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Fearnley et al, 2019).

claim: Afadin is recruited for dephosphorylation by directly binding to the PTPRK D2 pseudophosphatase domain.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Afadin is recruited for dephosphorylation by directly binding to the PTPRK D2 pseudophosphatase domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-2.

claim: The Afadin-PTPRK interaction is mapped to a putative coiled coil (CC) domain in Afadin that is separated by more than 100 amino acids from the substrate pTyr residue.
source: We mapped this interaction to a putative coiled coil (CC) domain in Afadin that is separated by more than 100 amino acids from the substrate pTyr residue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental mapping data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Afadin is selectively dephosphorylated by PTPRK yet not by the closely related receptor tyrosine phosphatase PTPRM.
source: We identify the residues that define PTP specificity, explaining how Afadin is selectively dephosphorylated by PTPRK yet not by the closely related receptor tyrosine phosphatase PTPRM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and structural predictions shown in Figure 4.

claim: PTP substrate specificity can be determined by protein–protein interactions distal to the active site.
source: Our work demonstrates that PTP substrate specificity can be determined by protein–protein interactions distal to the active site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing that the CC domain binding site is >100 amino acids from the phosphorylation site.

claim: PTPRK and other PTPs achieve substrate specificity despite a lack of specific sequence context at the substrate pTyr.
source: This explains how PTPRK and other PTPs achieve substrate specificity despite a lack of specific sequence context at the substrate pTyr.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that substrate recognition occurs through a domain distant from the phosphorylation site.

claim: The PTPRK-Afadin interactions are phosphorylation-independent and mediated via binding to a non-catalytic domain.
source: Furthermore, by demonstrating that these interactions are phosphorylation-independent and mediated via binding to a non-catalytic domain, we highlight how receptor PTPs could function as intracellular scaffolds in addition to catalyzing protein dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing binding occurs through the D2 pseudophosphatase domain.

claim: Receptor PTPs could function as intracellular scaffolds in addition to catalyzing protein dephosphorylation.
source: Furthermore, by demonstrating that these interactions are phosphorylation-independent and mediated via binding to a non-catalytic domain, we highlight how receptor PTPs could function as intracellular scaffolds in addition to catalyzing protein dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the phosphorylation-independent binding observed.

claim: Dysregulation of the balance between kinases and phosphatases is associated with disease, including tumor progression.
source: Dysregulation of this balance is associated with disease, including tumor progression (Arora and Scholar, 2005; Hunter and Sefton, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It has been challenging to develop PTP inhibitors due to their highly charged active sites and lack of selectivity at the peptide level.
source: It has been challenging to develop PTP inhibitors due to their highly charged active sites, as well as their lack of selectivity at the peptide level (Barr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: PTPs show marked substrate specificity in vivo despite a lack of specific consensus sequences for pTyr substrates.
source: Despite a lack of specific consensus sequences for pTyr substrates (Barr et al., 2009; Ren et al., 2011), PTPs show marked substrate specificity in vivo (Fearnley et al., 2019; Saxena et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PTPRK is a member of the R2B family of transmembrane receptor PTPs that supports cell adhesion and has been implicated as a tumor suppressor.
source: Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor-type kappa (PTPRK) is a member of the R2B family of transmembrane receptor (R)PTPs that supports cell adhesion and has been implicated as a tumor suppressor (Chang et al., 2020; McArdle et al., 2001; Shimozato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PTPRK possesses two intracellular PTP domains, one catalytically active proximal to the plasma membrane (D1) and a distal inactive pseudophosphatase (D2).
source: Like other receptor PTPs, PTPRK possesses two intracellular PTP domains, one catalytically active proximal to the plasma membrane (D1) and a distal inactive, pseudophosphatase (D2).
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on established knowledge of PTPRK.

claim: For several PTPRK substrates the active D1 PTP domain itself appears not to be the sole determinant of substrate binding.
source: We previously showed that for several PTPRK substrates the active D1 PTP domain itself appears not to be the sole determinant of substrate binding.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The inactive D2 domains of PTPRK and its paralog PTPRM have critical roles in substrate recruitment.
source: Instead, the inactive D2 domains of PTPRK and its paralog PTPRM were shown to have critical roles in substrate recruitment (Fearnley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Afadin (MLLT4/AF6) was identified as a PTPRK substrate and is recruited via the PTPRK D2 domain.
source: Specifically, we identified Afadin (MLLT4/AF6) as a PTPRK substrate and identified that it is recruited via the PTPRK D2 domain (Fearnley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Structural studies of the PTPRC-ICD suggested a potential role for the D2 domain in substrate recruitment.
source: In a similar paradigm, structural studies of the PTPRC-ICD suggested a potential role for the D2 domain in substrate recruitment (Nam et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The presence of the PTPRC-D2 is critical for the recruitment and dephosphorylation of several proposed substrates, including the T cell receptor and the Lck Src-family tyrosine kinase.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the presence of the PTPRC-D2 is critical for the recruitment and dephosphorylation of several proposed substrates, including the T cell receptor (Kashio et al., 1998) and the Lck Src-family tyrosine kinase (Felberg et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Afadin is a conserved junctional plaque protein, important for linking cell surface adhesion molecules to the cytoskeleton, and is regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Afadin is a conserved junctional plaque protein, important for linking cell surface adhesion molecules to the cytoskeleton, and is regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation (Niessen and Gottardi, 2008; Yu and Zallen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Afadin deletion in mice is embryonically lethal and leads to dysregulated junctions and polarity.
source: Afadin deletion in mice is embryonically lethal and leads to dysregulated junctions and polarity (Zhadanov et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Afadin is a large (>200 kDa) protein possessing multiple folded domains and extended regions of predicted disorder.
source: It is a large (>200 kDa) protein possessing multiple folded domains and extended regions of predicted disorder.
evidence: This is based on structural characterization and predictions.

claim: The annotation of Afadin domains in UniProt is in good agreement with predictions of ordered/structured regions as calculated by AlphaFold2 and IUPred3.
source: The annotation of these domains, as described in UniProt (UniProt ID: P55196), is in good agreement with predictions of ordered/structured regions as calculated by AlphaFold2 (AF2) and IUPred3 (Erdős et al., 2021; Jumper et al., 2021; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions and comparison with database annotations, shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Afadin's modular domain structure allows it to engage in multivalent interactions through distinct domains.
source: This modular domain structure allows Afadin to engage in multivalent interactions through distinct domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural organization of Afadin.

claim: Afadin is an effector of GTP-bound Ras, placing it downstream of activated receptor tyrosine kinases.
source: Afadin is an effector of GTP-bound Ras (Goudreault et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2017), placing it downstream of activated receptor tyrosine kinases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Afadin can play a structural role, linking adhesion receptors, such as nectins, to the actin cytoskeleton.
source: It can also play a structural role, linking adhesion receptors, such as nectins, to the actin cytoskeleton (Takai and Nakanishi, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Afadin's PDZ domain binds the plekstrin homology (PH) domain-containing adherens junction protein PLEKHA7.
source: It participates in additional scaffolding functions, for example, its PDZ domain binds the plekstrin homology (PH) domain-containing adherens junction protein PLEKHA7 (Kurita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Afadin's interaction with LGN was characterized structurally and showed binding to a C-terminal disordered region of Afadin, adjacent to its F-actin binding region.
source: Its interaction with LGN, a protein involved in spindle orientation during cytokinesis, was characterized structurally and showed binding to a C-terminal disordered region of Afadin, adjacent to its F-actin binding region (Carminati et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: Disordered regions of Afadin can engage in specific interactions via formation of elongated peptide interfaces along extended surfaces of partner proteins.
source: This structure clearly demonstrates that these disordered regions of Afadin can engage in specific interactions via formation of elongated peptide interfaces along extended surfaces of partner proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural characterization of Afadin-LGN interaction.

claim: Y1230 was identified as the putative target for dephosphorylation by the PTPRK D1 domain as it was hyperphosphorylated in PTPRK knockout cells.
source: Within one of these extended, disordered regions of Afadin lies residue Y1230, the tyrosine that was identified as the putative target for dephosphorylation by the PTPRK D1 domain as it was hyperphosphorylated in PTPRK knockout (KO) cells (Fearnley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Afadin is required for its interaction with SHP-2 and is important for downstream signaling by platelet-derived growth factor.
source: Phosphorylation of Afadin is required for its interaction with SHP-2 and is important for downstream signaling by platelet-derived growth factor (Nakata et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Afadin is an essential regulator of adherens junctions that mediates phosphorylation-dependent and multivalent protein–protein interactions.
source: Thus, Afadin is an essential regulator of adherens junctions that mediates phosphorylation-dependent and multivalent protein–protein interactions.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the cited literature about Afadin's functions.

claim: A band at the predicted molecular weight of the longest isoform of Afadin is detected at higher levels in PTPRK KO compared to WT MCF10A cells using the Afadin-pY1230 antibody.
source: Consistent with our previous tyrosine phosphoproteomics data, a band at the predicted molecular weight of the longest isoform of Afadin is detected at higher levels in PTPRK KO compared to WT MCF10A cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Afadin-pY1230 signal is increased by pervanadate treatment.
source: This band is increased by pervanadate (Huyer et al., 1997), a cell treatment that globally increases protein tyrosine phosphorylation, and is decreased by knockdown of Afadin using siRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and citation to previous literature.

claim: The Afadin-pY1230 signal is decreased by knockdown of Afadin using siRNA.
source: This band is increased by pervanadate (Huyer et al., 1997), a cell treatment that globally increases protein tyrosine phosphorylation, and is decreased by knockdown of Afadin using siRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Phosphorylation interferes with the signal when using an anti-Afadin (epitope: 1091–1233) antibody from BD Transduction Laboratories on immunoblots, resulting in decreased intensity when Afadin is phosphorylated.
source: It should be noted that phosphorylation appears to interfere with the signal when using an anti-Afadin (epitope: 1091–1233) antibody from BD Transduction Laboratories on immunoblots, resulting in decreased intensity when Afadin is phosphorylated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and C.

claim: Y1230 is the predominant phosphosite recognized by the Afadin-pY1230 antibody.
source: However, there was no detectable increase in signal upon pervanadate treatment of mScarlet-Afadin-Y1230F mutants, supporting that this is the predominant phosphosite recognized by our Afadin phosphoantibody.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Y1230F mutants.

claim: PTPRK-ICD, but not the PTPRK D1 domain alone, dephosphorylates Afadin.
source: We previously demonstrated that the PTPRK ICD, but not the PTPRK D1 domain alone, dephosphorylates Afadin (Fearnley et al., 2019). This is recapitulated using the pY1230 Afadin antibody after incubation of recombinant domains with pervanadate-treated, DTT-quenched, MCF10A lysates (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: PTPRK-ICD shows greater activity against Afadin pY1230 than PTPRK-D1 over a time course.
source: Over a time course, PTPRK-ICD shows greater activity against Afadin pY1230 than PTPRK-D1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time course experiments.

claim: p120Cat was dephosphorylated equally by PTPRK-ICD and PTPRK-D1 domains.
source: In contrast, p120Cat was dephosphorylated equally by the two domains, with minimal dephosphorylation of the non-substrate control, paxillin-pY118.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing substrate dephosphorylation.

claim: Paxillin-pY118 shows minimal dephosphorylation by PTPRK domains.
source: In contrast, p120Cat was dephosphorylated equally by the two domains, with minimal dephosphorylation of the non-substrate control, paxillin-pY118.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing paxillin as a non-substrate control.

claim: The hyperphosphorylation of Afadin Y1230 in PTPRK KO MCF10A cell lysates could be reduced by doxycycline-induced expression of PTPRK to wildtype levels, but not by a catalytically inactive mutant.
source: Finally, the observed hyperphosphorylation of Afadin Y1230 in PTPRK KO MCF10A cell lysates could be reduced by doxycycline-induced expression of PTPRK to wildtype levels, but not by a catalytically inactive mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: The Afadin-pY1230 antibody is specific to Afadin phosphorylated at Y1230.
source: Together, these data confirm that this new antibody is specific to Afadin phosphorylated at Y1230 and that pY1230 is targeted for dephosphorylation by PTPRK in a D2 domain-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental validations of the antibody.

claim: pY1230 is targeted for dephosphorylation by PTPRK in a D2 domain-dependent manner.
source: Together, these data confirm that this new antibody is specific to Afadin phosphorylated at Y1230 and that pY1230 is targeted for dephosphorylation by PTPRK in a D2 domain-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing the requirement of the D2 domain.

claim: Full-length Afadin binds to the PTPRK-ICD, consistent with a direct interaction.
source: We observed clear binding of full-length Afadin to the PTPRK-ICD (Figure 1C), consistent with a direct interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental pull-down data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of the Afadin C-terminal disordered tail was sufficient to abolish binding to PTPRK.
source: Deletion of the Afadin C-terminal disordered tail was sufficient to abolish binding to PTPRK (Figure 1D, aa. 1–1097).
evidence: This is supported by experimental truncation mapping data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A GST-fusion construct encompassing the entire C-terminal disordered region of Afadin showed direct binding to PTPRK.
source: A GST-fusion construct encompassing the entire C-terminal disordered region of Afadin, shown to be important in the wheat germ system, also showed direct binding to PTPRK, supporting the identification of this region as sufficient for binding (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental pull-down data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Only Afadin constructs containing a short, 63-residue predicted coiled-coil (CC) region spanning residues 1393–1455 were able to bind PTPRK.
source: Several truncation constructs within this region were tested for binding to PTPRK, clearly identifying that only constructs containing a short, 63-residue predicted coiled-coil (CC) region spanning residues 1393–1455 was able to bind PTPRK (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental truncation mapping data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The Afadin CC region (residues 1393–1455) is both necessary and sufficient for binding to the PTPRK-ICD.
source: Therefore, this CC region is both necessary and sufficient for binding to the PTPRK-ICD.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on truncation mapping experiments.

claim: The Afadin-CC region includes a high proportion of charged residues.
source: The sequence composition of this region of Afadin (Afadin-CC) includes a high proportion of charged residues (Figure 1F), suggesting that the PTPRK–Afadin interaction could be electrostatically mediated.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The PTPRK–Afadin interaction is sensitive to salt concentration.
source: In support of this, the PTPRK–Afadin interaction was sensitive to salt concentration, with less GST-Afadin-CC present in PTPRK pull-downs at increasing NaCl concentrations (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PTPRK-ICD and Afadin-CC have complementary predicted isoelectric points (pI = 5.3 and 10.2, respectively).
source: Further, PTPRK-ICD and Afadin-CC have complementary predicted isoelectric points (pI = 5.3 and 10.2, respectively), suggesting that these fragments would retain charge complementarity at physiological pH.
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of isoelectric points.

claim: The PTPRK-ICD interacts directly and specifically with the C-terminal Afadin-CC region.
source: Together, these data show that the PTPRK-ICD interacts directly and specifically with the C-terminal Afadin-CC region.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: The Afadin-CC is a monomer with a molecular mass of ~8 kDa.
source: This technique allows for the direct measurement of the molar mass of a particle in solution and demonstrated that the Afadin-CC is a monomer, with a molecular mass of ~8 kDa (predicted mass = 8.3 kDa, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Following removal of the GST tag, the Afadin-CC region may be prone to some degradation.
source: The chromatography trace also revealed a small amount of truncated Afadin-CC, suggesting that following removal of the GST tag this region may be prone to some degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on SEC-MALS chromatography data.

claim: Afadin-CC forms an equimolar complex with PTPRK-ICD with a binding affinity of KD = 3.2 ± 0.6 µM.
source: Afadin-CC (without the GST tag) forms an equimolar complex with PTPRK-ICD with a binding affinity in the low micromolar range (KD = 3.2 ± 0.6 µM, Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 2B and E.

claim: The binding affinity of Afadin-CC to PTPRK-ICD is consistent with a reversible, transient protein–protein interaction as expected for an enzyme-substrate complex.
source: This binding affinity is consistent with a reversible, transient protein–protein interaction as expected for an enzyme-substrate complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measured binding affinity.

claim: The high ΔH of the PTPRK-ICD:Afadin-CC interaction (–17.6 ± 0.7 kcal/mol) indicates it is enthalpically driven.
source: The high ΔH of this interaction (–17.6 ± 0.7 kcal/mol) indicates it is enthalpically driven, consistent with the highly charged nature of the Afadin-CC region.
evidence: This is based on ITC experimental data and thermodynamic interpretation.

claim: The PTPRK-D2 domain alone is sufficient to bind Afadin-CC to similar levels observed for the full ICD.
source: The PTPRK-D2 domain alone was sufficient to bind Afadin-CC to similar levels observed for the full ICD (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental pull-down data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No interaction of Afadin-CC with the PTPRK-D1 domain was observed.
source: No interaction of Afadin-CC with the PTPRK-D1 domain was observed, highlighting that the D2 domain is necessary and sufficient for the interaction with this part of Afadin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental pull-down data.

claim: The D2 domain is necessary and sufficient for the interaction with Afadin-CC.
source: No interaction of Afadin-CC with the PTPRK-D1 domain was observed, highlighting that the D2 domain is necessary and sufficient for the interaction with this part of Afadin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental pull-down data.

claim: Afadin-CC forms an equimolar complex with the PTPRK-D2 domain with a binding affinity of KD = 6.3 ± 0.3 µM.
source: These data produced very similar results to those for the full ICD, specifically the Afadin-CC forms an equimolar complex with the PTPRK-D2 domain with a binding affinity in the low micromolar range (KD = 6.3 ± 0.3 µM, Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: There is only a very modest (twofold) reduction in binding affinity for the D2 domain when compared with the ICD.
source: These data suggest there is only a very modest (twofold) reduction in binding affinity for the D2 domain when compared with the ICD, consistent with the D2 domain being the primary Afadin binding surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of ITC data for ICD and D2 domain.

claim: The D2 domain is the primary Afadin binding surface.
source: These data suggest there is only a very modest (twofold) reduction in binding affinity for the D2 domain when compared with the ICD, consistent with the D2 domain being the primary Afadin binding surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on ITC binding affinity measurements.

claim: Many residues at both the N- and C-termini of the Afadin-CC may not be contributing to the putative interaction interface with PTPRK-D2.
source: The AF2 model of PTPRK-D2 in complex with the full Afadin-CC fragment used for biochemical characterization highlighted that many residues at both the N- and C-termini of the Afadin-CC may not be contributing to the putative interaction interface (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AF2 structural prediction shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Regions at both the N- and C-termini of Afadin-CC are dispensable for the interaction with PTPRK.
source: In agreement with the initial AF2 model, regions at both the N- and C-termini of Afadin-CC were dispensable for the interaction, while disruption of the core sequence encompassing the charged residues (aa. 1408–1448) resulted in a lack of detectable binding (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental truncation mapping data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Disruption of the core sequence encompassing the charged residues (aa. 1408–1448) of Afadin-CC resulted in a lack of detectable binding to PTPRK.
source: In agreement with the initial AF2 model, regions at both the N- and C-termini of Afadin-CC were dispensable for the interaction, while disruption of the core sequence encompassing the charged residues (aa. 1408–1448) resulted in a lack of detectable binding (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental truncation mapping data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The core charged region of Afadin (aa. 1408–1448) is almost completely conserved across vertebrates and diverges in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Interestingly, this core charged region of Afadin is almost completely conserved across vertebrates and diverges in Drosophila melanogaster, which lacks a full-length PTPRK ortholog (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Hatzihristidis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster lacks a full-length PTPRK ortholog.
source: Interestingly, this core charged region of Afadin is almost completely conserved across vertebrates and diverges in Drosophila melanogaster, which lacks a full-length PTPRK ortholog (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Hatzihristidis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The top AF2 model predicts the Afadin-CC adopts a linear alpha-helical structure that stretches across one face of the D2 domain.
source: Of the five models calculated, the top four had the Afadin-CC placed in the same position on the surface of the PTPRK-D2 domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), strongly suggesting that the CC domain adopts a linear alpha-helical structure that stretches across one face of the D2 domain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on AF2 structural predictions shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The top AF2 model predicts the overall fold of each domain with high confidence and their relative orientations with moderate to high confidence.
source: The top AF2 model (ipTM + pTM score = 0.58) predicts the overall fold of each domain with high confidence and their relative orientations with moderate to high confidence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on AF2 prediction quality metrics shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Double alanine mutation at Afadin residues W1418-Y1419 abolishes binding to PTPRK.
source: Double alanine mutation at Afadin residues W1418-Y1419 or R1432-K1433, which contribute large sidechains to the interaction interface, abolishes binding to PTPRK, while E1429-R1430 to alanine reduces but does not abolish binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Double alanine mutation at Afadin residues R1432-K1433 abolishes binding to PTPRK.
source: Double alanine mutation at Afadin residues W1418-Y1419 or R1432-K1433, which contribute large sidechains to the interaction interface, abolishes binding to PTPRK, while E1429-R1430 to alanine reduces but does not abolish binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: E1429-R1430 to alanine mutation in Afadin reduces but does not abolish binding to PTPRK.
source: Double alanine mutation at Afadin residues W1418-Y1419 or R1432-K1433, which contribute large sidechains to the interaction interface, abolishes binding to PTPRK, while E1429-R1430 to alanine reduces but does not abolish binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutations to Afadin residues distal from the interface (R1410, Q1443, T1446) do not interfere with binding to PTPRK.
source: Importantly, additional mutations to residues distal from the interface (R1410, Q1443, T1446) do not interfere with binding to PTPRK.
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The mutational data strongly support the validity of the predicted structure for how Afadin binds to the PTPRK D2 domain.
source: These mutational data strongly support the validity of the predicted structure for how Afadin binds to the PTPRK D2 domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the agreement between AF2 predictions and experimental mutagenesis data.

claim: Both PTPRK and PTPRU bind Afadin while PTPRM cannot.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that both PTPRK and PTPRU bind Afadin while PTPRM cannot (Fearnley et al., 2019; Hay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Residues on the D2 domain that are critical for Afadin binding should be conserved in PTPRK and PTPRU but divergent in PTPRM.
source: Therefore, residues on the D2 domain that are critical for Afadin binding should be conserved in PTPRK and PTPRU but divergent in PTPRM.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the differential binding specificity.

claim: A cluster of four residues mapped to a region of the PTPRK-D2 surface that is predicted to be the binding site for Afadin-CC.
source: Interestingly, a cluster of four residues mapped to a region of the PTPRK-D2 surface that is predicted to be the binding site for Afadin-CC (Figure 4A) and are located adjacent to several Afadin-CC residues that we have shown to be necessary for complex formation (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and mapping onto the AF2 structural model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Afadin-CC binding site on PTPRK-D2 is located on the opposite face relative to the cysteine of the would-be 'active' site in the PTPRK-D2 domain.
source: This binding site is located on the opposite face relative to the cysteine of the would-be 'active' site in the PTPRK-D2 domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the AF2 structural model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PTPRK residues Y1270, G1273, E1332, and L1335 form an acidic pocket into which the Afadin-CC is predicted to bind.
source: Although these residues of PTPRK (Y1270, G1273, E1332, and L1335) are not all highly charged, within the context of the PTPRK model they form an acidic pocket into which the Afadin-CC is predicted to bind (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on the AF2 structural model and electrostatic analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: In a model of the PTPRM-D2, the altered residues result in a different surface topology and charge, having lost the acidic pocket observed for PTPRK-D2.
source: Strikingly, in a model of the PTPRM-D2 the altered residues in this region result in a different surface topology and charge, having lost the acidic pocket observed for PTPRK-D2 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on AF2 structural modeling and electrostatic analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Changes in surface properties between PTPRK-D2 and PTPRM-D2 may account for the differential binding to Afadin.
source: These changes in surface properties may therefore account for the differential binding to Afadin.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling and known binding specificities.

claim: PTPRK-G1273H single-point mutation is sufficient to abolish the interaction of the PTPRK-D2 with GST-Afadin-CC.
source: Each of these single-point mutations were sufficient to abolish the interaction of the PTPRK-D2 with the GST-Afadin-CC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PTPRK-L1335R single-point mutation is sufficient to abolish the interaction of the PTPRK-D2 with GST-Afadin-CC.
source: Each of these single-point mutations were sufficient to abolish the interaction of the PTPRK-D2 with the GST-Afadin-CC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Introduction of both G1273H and L1335R mutations (double mutant) into the PTPRK-D2 or full PTPRK-ICD prevents binding to Afadin-CC.
source: Furthermore, the introduction of both mutations (double mutant [DM]) into the PTPRK-D2 or full PTPRK-ICD prevents binding to Afadin-CC (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No binding was detected between PTPRK-D2-DM and Afadin-CC by ITC, confirming loss of the interaction.
source: To quantify the loss in affinity due to these point mutations, ITC binding experiments were repeated using the PTPRK-D2-DM with Afadin-CC and no binding was detected, confirming loss of the interaction (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Introduction of G1273H/L1335R mutations into PTPRK reduces Afadin binding to background levels in wheat germ lysate pull-downs.
source: While PTPRK-ICD and PTPRK-D2 bind Afadin, introduction of these two mutations into PTPRK reduces Afadin binding to background levels (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental pull-down data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: PTPRK-F1225A single-point mutation vastly reduces binding to the Afadin-CC domain.
source: This single-point mutation (F1225A) in PTPRK-D2 vastly reduces binding to the Afadin-CC domain (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: PTPRK-F1225 is conserved across the R2B family and contributes to binding affinity but not specificity.
source: This residue is conserved across the R2B family so although it contributes to the binding affinity and validates the complex model, it does not contribute to specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation and mutagenesis data.

claim: The M-loop mutation (CEE to YNG) in PTPRK retains binding to Afadin-CC.
source: This mutation retains binding, suggesting that this loop does not contribute to specificity of Afadin binding to PTPRK versus PTPRM (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The M-loop does not contribute to specificity of Afadin binding to PTPRK versus PTPRM.
source: This mutation retains binding, suggesting that this loop does not contribute to specificity of Afadin binding to PTPRK versus PTPRM (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis data showing retained binding.

claim: Wildtype and mutant PTPRK-D2 domains possessed Tm values between 39 and 41°C, supporting that any loss of binding was not driven by misfolding.
source: Wildtype and mutant PTPRK-D2 domains possessed Tm values between 39 and 41°C, supporting that any loss of binding was not driven by misfolding.
evidence: This is supported by DSF experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mutational data strongly validate the predicted model for the PTPRK-D2:Afadin-CC complex.
source: These data strongly validate the predicted model for the PTPRK-D2:Afadin-CC complex and identify two key residues within PTPRK D2 that are crucial for binding to full-length Afadin and, based on their lack of conservation in PTPRM, are likely to be important for determining binding specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the agreement between predictions and experimental mutagenesis data.

claim: G1273 and L1335 are two key residues within PTPRK D2 that are crucial for binding to full-length Afadin and likely important for determining binding specificity.
source: These data strongly validate the predicted model for the PTPRK-D2:Afadin-CC complex and identify two key residues within PTPRK D2 that are crucial for binding to full-length Afadin and, based on their lack of conservation in PTPRM, are likely to be important for determining binding specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis data and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: WT and DM PTPRK-ICDs have identical activity profiles using the generic phosphatase substrate pNPP.
source: The WT and DM PTPRK-ICDs were compared in activity assays using the generic phosphatase substrate 4-nitrophenyl phosphate (pNPP), which confirmed that both proteins have identical activity profiles (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental phosphatase activity assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Afadin was dephosphorylated at Y1230 by WT PTPRK-ICD, but not PTPRK-ICD DM.
source: Afadin was dephosphorylated at Y1230 by WT PTPRK-ICD, but not PTPRK-ICD DM (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental dephosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: p120-Catenin was dephosphorylated by both WT and DM PTPRK-ICD proteins – independent of D2 domain mutation status.
source: Comparatively, another PTPRK substrate, p120-Catenin, which has been shown previously to be dephosphorylated efficiently by the PTPRK-D1 domain alone, was dephosphorylated by both proteins – independent of D2 domain mutation status.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dephosphorylation assay data.

claim: Afadin was depleted in pTyr-IPs from lysates treated with WT PTPRK-ICD, showing dephosphorylation had occurred.
source: Afadin was depleted in pTyr-IPs from lysates treated with WT PTPRK-ICD, showing dephosphorylation had occurred, while the levels of phosphorylated Afadin remained unchanged in PTPRK-ICD DM-treated samples (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The levels of phosphorylated Afadin remained unchanged in PTPRK-ICD DM-treated samples.
source: Afadin was depleted in pTyr-IPs from lysates treated with WT PTPRK-ICD, showing dephosphorylation had occurred, while the levels of phosphorylated Afadin remained unchanged in PTPRK-ICD DM-treated samples (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both WT and DM PTPRK were equivalently able to dephosphorylate p120-Catenin in pTyr-IP experiments.
source: Again, both WT and DM PTPRK were equivalently able to dephosphorylate p120-Catenin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: D2 domain recruitment of Afadin is critical for efficient dephosphorylation by the D1 domain.
source: These data show that D2 domain recruitment of Afadin is critical for efficient dephosphorylation by the D1 domain, and that PTPRK uses distinct surfaces to recruit different substrates for dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential dephosphorylation of Afadin by WT vs DM PTPRK.

claim: PTPRK uses distinct surfaces to recruit different substrates for dephosphorylation.
source: These data show that D2 domain recruitment of Afadin is critical for efficient dephosphorylation by the D1 domain, and that PTPRK uses distinct surfaces to recruit different substrates for dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential requirement of the D2 domain for Afadin vs p120-Catenin dephosphorylation.

claim: The interaction between Afadin and PTPRK-D2 was independent of phosphorylation using whole-cell lysates.
source: Using whole-cell lysates, we previously reported that the interaction between Afadin and PTPRK-D2 was independent of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The interaction with the Afadin CC region is critical for bringing Afadin within close proximity to PTPRK but does not directly position the relevant pTyr in the active site of the PTPRK-D1 domain.
source: We also demonstrate that the interaction with the CC region is critical for efficient dephosphorylation, showing that this interaction is important for bringing Afadin within close proximity to PTPRK but does not directly position the relevant pTyr in the active site of the PTPRK-D1 domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the distance between the CC binding site and the phosphorylation site.

claim: The role for the D2 pseudophosphatase domain in specific substrate recruitment helps to explain the apparent lack of specificity of phosphatases for phosphopeptide substrates.
source: This role for the D2 pseudophosphatase domain in specific substrate recruitment helps to explain the apparent lack of specificity of phosphatases for phosphopeptide substrates, indicating that it is not necessarily a motif near the pTyr that determines substrate targeting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about D2-mediated substrate recruitment.

claim: It is not necessarily a motif near the pTyr that determines substrate targeting by PTPs.
source: This role for the D2 pseudophosphatase domain in specific substrate recruitment helps to explain the apparent lack of specificity of phosphatases for phosphopeptide substrates, indicating that it is not necessarily a motif near the pTyr that determines substrate targeting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about distal binding sites.

claim: Afadin binds PTPRK via a site that is over 100 amino acids downstream of the target phosphosite.
source: Specifically, Afadin binds PTPRK via a site that is over 100 amino acids downstream of the target phosphosite and the interaction interface is distinct from the nonfunctional 'active site' on the D2 domain.
evidence: This is based on the mapping data showing the CC domain location relative to Y1230.

claim: The Afadin-PTPRK interaction interface is distinct from the nonfunctional 'active site' on the D2 domain.
source: Specifically, Afadin binds PTPRK via a site that is over 100 amino acids downstream of the target phosphosite and the interaction interface is distinct from the nonfunctional 'active site' on the D2 domain.
evidence: This is based on the structural model showing the binding site location.

claim: The pseudophosphatase domain has been repurposed in evolution for specific protein–protein interactions.
source: These data support that the pseudophosphatase domain has been repurposed in evolution for specific protein–protein interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings about D2 domain function.

claim: It is possible that even active PTP domains mediate protein-protein interactions similar to pseudophosphatase domains.
source: However, it is also possible that even active PTP domains mediate such interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about potential broader implications.

claim: Additional substrates, such as PARD3, showed some dependence on the D2 for dephosphorylation by PTPRK and PTPRM.
source: Additional substrates, such as PARD3, showed some dependence on the D2 for dephosphorylation by PTPRK and PTPRM, whereas other substrates of PTPRK, such as p120Cat, do not require the D2 domain for recruitment (Fearnley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: p120Cat does not require the D2 domain for recruitment to PTPRK.
source: Additional substrates, such as PARD3, showed some dependence on the D2 for dephosphorylation by PTPRK and PTPRM, whereas other substrates of PTPRK, such as p120Cat, do not require the D2 domain for recruitment (Fearnley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: If the phosphorylation state is not critical for binding, PTPRK might play a scaffolding role connecting multiple junctional components as well as F-actin.
source: Furthermore, if the phosphorylation state is not critical for binding, PTPRK might play a scaffolding role connecting multiple junctional components as well as F-actin.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phosphorylation-independent binding observed.

claim: Structural studies on the R2A receptor PTPRF revealed an interaction interface with Liprin-α spanning both the D1 and D2 domains.
source: Consistent with a scaffolding role for receptor PTPs, structural studies on the R2A receptor PTPRF revealed an interaction interface with Liprin-α spanning both the D1 and D2 domains, adding further complexity to potential binding modes (Xie et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: Liprin is not a PTPRF substrate.
source: Interestingly, Liprin is not a PTPRF substrate, thus RPTPs could form multiprotein complexes independent of protein phosphorylation status.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on previous knowledge.

claim: RPTPs could form multiprotein complexes independent of protein phosphorylation status.
source: Interestingly, Liprin is not a PTPRF substrate, thus RPTPs could form multiprotein complexes independent of protein phosphorylation status.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Liprin-PTPRF interaction.

claim: RPTPs have reported phosphatase-independent functions.
source: This might also help to explain reported phosphatase-independent functions of RPTPs (Juettner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The region of Afadin that interacts with PTPRK has been shown to also mediate binding to αE-catenin.
source: Finally, the region of Afadin that interacts with PTPRK has been shown to also mediate binding to αE-catenin (Maruo et al., 2018), a core component of the E cadherin-catenin complex (Niessen and Gottardi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: αE-catenin is a core component of the E cadherin-catenin complex.
source: Finally, the region of Afadin that interacts with PTPRK has been shown to also mediate binding to αE-catenin (Maruo et al., 2018), a core component of the E cadherin-catenin complex (Niessen and Gottardi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.
